Harp

HARP -- same spelling as the musical instrument, but here always used as a verb, as in 'to harp on' something. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To harp to discuss or complain about something excessively and tediously (used with 'on').

Even after the team won the championship, the assistant coach continued to harp on the one play that had gone wrong in the third quarter.

Worked Example

A father whose daughter got an A- on one quiz keeps bringing it up at dinner every night for two straight weeks, even after she's since earned three A's in a row.

That tedious, repeated fixation on one small issue long after it matters is exactly what it means to harp on something. Unlike 'mention,' which can happen once, harp on implies wearisome repetition.

How Harp Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

dwell

dwell: to think or talk about something for a long time

belabor

belabor: to argue or worry over a point excessively

nag: to persistently pester someone about something

Antonyms

drop

drop: to stop discussing or pursuing a subject

overlook

overlook: to fail to notice or deliberately not mention something

How Strong Is It? — dwell → harp → belabor

dwell vs. harp

dwell vs. harp: Dwell is milder than harp -- to dwell on something can simply mean thinking about it too long, while to harp on it means repeating the complaint out loud, again and again.

belabor vs. harp

belabor vs. harp: Belabor can feel even more exhausting than harp: harping on something is usually one recurring gripe, while belaboring a point means arguing it at excessive, repetitive length.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — harp-

root — harp-: a plucked stringed musical instrument (Old English (hearpe))

Put it together

Put it together: Harp began as the name of the stringed instrument. The verb sense grew from the image of a musician plucking the very same string over and over -- to 'harp on' something is to keep striking the same note again and again, just as this word's own history keeps circling back to its literal musical root.

Use the root in a new word: harpsichord

Use the root in a new word: harpsichord: The harpsichord's plucked strings gave Baroque music its bright, percussive sound.
